skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings. Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. // UserFrame / Upool - Specifications
5. //
6. // `UserFrame` is an RAII owning handle to one reference of a reference-counted
7. // physical user frame, abstracted by the physical address of the frame it owns
8. // (`UserFrame@ : int`, defined by the `View` impl in `upool.rs`). `Upool` is a
9. // stateless allocation facade with no caller-observable state, so it has no
10. // `View`.
11. //
12. // All mutable state (which frames are allocated, and per-frame refcounts) lives
13. // in the do-not-modify `FrameAllocView` reached through `phys_view()`
14. // (`mod.spec.rs`). Because `phys_view()` is a zero-argument uninterpreted spec
15. // function (a single fixed value at the current program point), the frame
16. // allocator's effect is expressed as monotone single-state facts over
17. // `phys_view().frames`, exactly like the `frame::*` / `PhysMemoryManager::*`
18. // shim contracts -- there is no `old(phys_view())` to state a before/after
19. // transition against.
20. 
21. verus! {
22. 
23. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
24. use crate::mm::phys::phys_view;
25. 
26. impl UserFrame {
27.     /// A user-frame handle is well-formed iff the frame it names is
28.     /// page-aligned: it denotes a real physical frame, not an arbitrary byte.
29.     ///
30.     /// This is the only abstraction-level fact provable about a handle in
31.     /// isolation. Stronger facts -- "this frame is currently allocated", "its
32.     /// refcount is `n`" -- are properties of `phys_view().frames` keyed by
33.     /// `self@`, not invariants of the handle (a sibling `share`/`drop` changes
34.     /// them without changing this handle), so they are stated in
35.     /// `requires`/`ensures` over `phys_view()` instead.
36.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
37.         self@ % spec_page_size() == 0
38.     }
39. }
40. 
41. } // verus!
42.

1. // Copyright(c) The Maintainers of Nanvix.
2. // Licensed under the MIT License.
3. 
4. //==================================================================================================
5. // Imports
6. //==================================================================================================
7. 
8. use vstd::prelude::*;
9. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
10. include!("upool.spec.rs");
11. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
12. include!("upool.proof.rs");
13. 
14. use crate::{
15.     hal::mem::FrameAddress,
16.     mm::phys::frame,
17. };
18. use ::core::mem::ManuallyDrop;
19. use ::sys::error::Error;
20. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
21. use ::vstd::prelude::*;
22. 
23. //==================================================================================================
24. // User Frame
25. //==================================================================================================
26. 
27. ///
28. /// # Description
29. ///
30. /// A type that represents a user frame.
31. ///
32. #[derive(Debug)]
33. #[verus_verify]
34. pub struct UserFrame {
35.     /// Frame address.
36.     addr: FrameAddress,
37. }
38. 
39. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
40. verus! {
41. 
42. /// Abstract view of a [`UserFrame`]: the physical address of the frame it owns.
43. ///
44. /// Lets allocator contracts name a returned user frame's address (e.g. "the
45. /// returned frame is now allocated") without exposing any storage detail.
46. impl View for UserFrame {
47.     type V = int;
48. 
49.     closed spec fn view(&self) -> int {
50.         self.addr@
51.     }
52. }
53. 
54. } // verus!
55. 
56. #[verus_verify]
57. impl UserFrame {
58.     ///
59.     /// # Description
60.     ///
61.     /// Instantiates a user frame.
62.     ///
63.     /// # Parameters
64.     ///
65.     /// - `addr`: Frame address.
66.     ///
67.     /// # Returns
68.     ///
69.     /// A user frame.
70.     ///
71.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
72.         requires
73.             addr.inv(),
74.         ensures
75.             // `new` merely names an existing frame: the handle's address is `addr`
76.             // and it inherits `addr`'s page-alignment. No allocation and no
77.             // refcount change occur (ownership semantics come from `Drop`/`leak`),
78.             // so `new` says nothing about `phys_view()`.
79.             ret@ == addr@,
80.             ret.inv(),
81.     )]
82.     pub fn new(addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
83.         Self { addr }
84.     }
85. 
86.     ///
87.     /// # Description
88.     ///
89.     /// Returns the physical address of the target user frame.
90.     ///
91.     /// # Returns
92.     ///
93.     /// The physical address of the target user frame.
94.     ///
95.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
96.         ensures
97.             // Pure getter: returns exactly the address the handle owns.
98.             ret@ == self@,
99.     )]
100.     pub fn address(&self) -> FrameAddress {
101.         self.addr
102.     }
103. 
104.     ///
105.     /// # Description
106.     ///
107.     /// Consumes the user frame without freeing the underlying physical frame.
108.     ///
109.     /// # Returns
110.     ///
111.     /// The frame address.
112.     ///
113.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
114.         ensures
115.             // Consumes the handle and returns its address without releasing the
116.             // reference: `Drop` is suppressed (via `ManuallyDrop`), so the frame
117.             // stays allocated and `phys_view()` is unchanged.
118.             ret@ == self@,
119.     )]
120.     pub fn leak(self) -> FrameAddress {
121.         let this: ManuallyDrop<Self> = ManuallyDrop::new(self);
122.         this.addr
123.     }
124. 
125.     ///
126.     /// # Description
127.     ///
128.     /// Adds a new reference to the underlying physical frame and returns a fresh
129.     /// [`UserFrame`] handle that owns that reference. The two handles share the
130.     /// same physical frame, and the frame is only reclaimed once both handles are
131.     /// dropped.
132.     ///
133.     /// This is the building block for copy-on-write sharing: the parent retains
134.     /// its handle, the child receives the returned handle.
135.     ///
136.     /// # Returns
137.     ///
138.     /// On success, a new [`UserFrame`] that aliases the same physical frame as
139.     /// `self`. On failure, an error is returned.
140.     ///
141.     #[verus_spec(child =>
142.         requires
143.             self.inv(),
144.             phys_view().initialized,
145.             phys_view().inv(),
146.         ensures
147.             phys_view().inv(),
148.             phys_view().initialized,
149.             // On success: a fresh handle aliasing the same physical frame (equal
150.             // view), well-formed, and the frame is still allocated (it has gained
151.             // a reference). On failure: no reference acquired; `self` is untouched.
152.             match child {
153.                 Ok(handle) => {
154.                     &&& handle@ == self@
155.                     &&& handle.inv()
156.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(handle@)
157.                 },
158.                 Err(_) => true,
159.             },
160.     )]
161.     pub fn share(&self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
162.         frame::share(self.addr)?;
163.         Ok(Self { addr: self.addr })
164.     }
165. 
166.     ///
167.     /// # Description
168.     ///
169.     /// Returns the current reference count of the underlying physical frame.
170.     ///
171.     /// # Returns
172.     ///
173.     /// Upon success, the current reference count of the underlying physical frame is returned.
174.     /// Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
175.     ///
176.     #[verus_spec(result =>
177.         requires
178.             self.inv(),
179.             phys_view().initialized,
180.             phys_view().inv(),
181.         ensures
182.             phys_view().inv(),
183.             phys_view().initialized,
184.             // Pure query of the underlying frame's reference count: neither
185.             // consumes `self` nor changes the count. On success the frame is
186.             // allocated and the returned count equals its refcount; on failure the
187.             // frame is not allocated.
188.             match result {
189.                 Ok(count) => {
190.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@)
191.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts.contains_key(self@)
192.                     &&& count as int == phys_view().frames.refcounts[self@]
193.                 },
194.                 Err(_) => !phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(self@),
195.             },
196.     )]
197.     pub fn refcount(&self) -> Result<u8, Error> {
198.         frame::refcount(self.addr)
199.     }
200. }
201. 
202. #[verus_verify]
203. impl Drop for UserFrame {
204.     #[verus_spec(
205.         ensures
206.             // Releasing a reference preserves the subsystem invariant (the last
207.             // reference returns the frame to the free pool). The precise refcount
208.             // transition is not expressible: `phys_view()` is a single fixed value
209.             // with no `old(phys_view())` to compare against. Errors are logged, not
210.             // propagated, so `drop` cannot unwind.
211.             phys_view().inv(),
212.         opens_invariants none
213.         no_unwind
214.     )]
215.     fn drop(&mut self) {
216.         if let Err(e) = frame::free(self.addr) {
217.             error!("failed to free user frame: {:?}", e);
218.         }
219.     }
220. }
221. 
222. //==================================================================================================
223. // User Frame Pool
224. //==================================================================================================
225. 
226. ///
227. /// # Description
228. ///
229. /// Thin facade over the module-level [`frame`](super::frame) allocator. Exists as a distinct type
230. /// so user-frame allocation has its own entry point ([`Upool::alloc`] returning [`UserFrame`]).
231. ///
232. #[derive(Debug)]
233. #[verus_verify]
234. pub struct Upool {
235.     /// Private field prevents external construction.
236.     _private: (),
237. }
238. 
239. #[verus_verify]
240. impl Upool {
241.     ///
242.     /// # Description
243.     ///
244.     /// Instantiates a user frame pool.
245.     ///
246.     /// # Returns
247.     ///
248.     /// A user frame pool.
249.     ///
250.     #[verus_verify]
251.     pub(super) fn new() -> Self {
252.         Self { _private: () }
253.     }
254. 
255.     ///
256.     /// # Description
257.     ///
258.     /// Allocates a single user frame from the user frame pool.
259.     ///
260.     /// # Returns
261.     ///
262.     /// Upon success, a user frame is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
263.     ///
264.     #[verus_spec(result =>
265.         requires
266.             phys_view().initialized,
267.             phys_view().inv(),
268.         ensures
269.             phys_view().inv(),
270.             phys_view().initialized,
271.             // On success: a handle owning a freshly allocated, page-aligned frame
272.             // whose address is now reserved (`allocated_frames`) with a single
273.             // reference. On failure: nothing is reported about the absent frame.
274.             match result {
275.                 Ok(uf) => {
276.                     &&& uf.inv()
277.                     &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.contains(uf@)
278.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts.contains_key(uf@)
279.                     &&& phys_view().frames.refcounts[uf@] == 1
280.                 },
281.                 Err(_) => true,
282.             },
283.     )]
284.     pub fn alloc(&mut self) -> Result<UserFrame, Error> {
285.         let addr: FrameAddress = frame::alloc()?;
286.         Ok(UserFrame::new(addr))
287.     }
288. }
289.

# Build Nanvix

Use this skill when the user asks to build, compile, format, lint, or spell-check Nanvix. This
covers all build-system operations exposed through the `z` utility.

## Prerequisites

- Development environment set up per `doc/setup.md`.
- A local cross-compilation toolchain (`toolchain/`).
- **Windows 11:** GNU Make on PATH, Windows Hypervisor Platform enabled,
  Developer Mode enabled, and Rust toolchain installed. See `doc/setup.md` for details.

## Windows Setup Summary

Before building on Windows, ensure:

1. **Windows Hypervisor Platform** is enabled (`Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform -All`, then reboot).
2. **Developer Mode** is on (Settings > Privacy & Security > For developers).
3. **GNU Make** is on PATH (`winget install ezwinports.make`).
4. **Rust toolchain** is installed via `winget install Rustlang.Rustup`.
5. Repository was cloned with `git clone -c core.symlinks=true`.
6. Git hooks are installed: `./z.ps1 setup`.

## Building

### Preferred Build Commands (using `z` utility)

```bash
# Build everything with the local toolchain.
./z build -- all
```

### Building Individual Components

```bash
# Kernel only.
./z build -- kernel
# Nanvixd only.
./z build -- all-nanvixd
# UserVM only.
./z build -- all-uservm
```

### Build Parameters

Set these as environment variables or pass them after `--` in the `z` command:

| Parameter        | Values                   | Default         |
|------------------|--------------------------|-----------------|
| `MACHINE`        | `microvm`                | `microvm`       |
| `TARGET`         | `x86`                    | `x86`           |
| `RELEASE`        | `yes`, `no`              | `no`            |
| `LOG_LEVEL`      | `trace`, `debug`,        | `error`         |
|                  | `info`, `warn`,          |                 |
|                  | `error`, `panic`         |                 |
===VERIFYCMD===
